paras: The attempted lynching of Alonzo Garner took place in St. Paul, Minnesota, on Sunday night, December 18, 1881, when a crowd nearly lynched Garner after he was arrested on a charge of setting several fires near the Post Siding. Garner survived, was indicted for arson, and was convicted the next month of attempting to burn a store. The only report of the attempt on him was a single clause in the St. Paul Daily Globe's police-court column, and no paper gave his race.

According to testimony in the municipal court, several buildings near the Post Siding were set on fire on Sunday night, and witnesses said they had seen Garner near the fires just before the alarm. A witness named Bender testified that Garner had said he was going to burn up the town. Witnesses also described his arrest, "after which he was almost lynched by the populace"; the report gave no details of what the crowd did, how large it was, or how he was protected.

When Garner appeared before Judge Burr in the municipal court the next afternoon, the Globe described him as "ragged to the verge of nakedness, unkempt, whisky soaked, and bloody." He said that he had "the tremens" and did not know what he was doing, and he was held to the grand jury on a charge of arson.

His case was among thirteen bound over from the municipal court when the January term of the district court opened, and the grand jury indicted him for arson. Before Judge Brill he pleaded not guilty and was remanded. On January 24, 1882, the district court tried him on one of four counts, attempting to burn the store of Chas Jabuke, in a case the Globe now described as setting fire to several buildings near Seventh street bridge; the jury returned a guilty verdict and he was remanded.
No report of anyone being arrested or charged over the attempt on Garner appears in the coverage, and no report of his sentence was found.

Coverage came only from the St. Paul Daily Globe, and only its first item mentioned the near-lynching, in passing, within a paragraph that called Garner "the fire bug" and dwelt on his appearance. The paper neither condemned nor approved the crowd, and its later court notices treated Garner as an ordinary arson defendant without referring to the crowd again. None of these items mentioned race.
